newsitem.title: UK: British public debt on track despite December blip.
newsitem.headline: British public debt on track despite December blip.

text.p: Britain's public sector deficit nearly doubled most forecasts in December but economists said the government's target for the financial year remains within reach.

Britain's public sector borrowing requirement totalled 2.12 billion pounds ($3.56 billion) last month, the Office for National Statistics said on Friday. City economists had forecast a shortfall only a little above one billion pounds.
That left a cumulative debt of 16.1 billion pounds for the first nine months of the year, still well below the 23 billion gap between government spending and revenue at the same stage last year.
"The deficit was higher than the market expected but the gloom should not be overdone," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy. "The target is still just about achievable."
In his November budget, Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke set a revised target of 26.4 billion pounds for Britain's PSBR in the current financial year.

A Treasury spokesman said Friday's figures were "entirely consistent" with the government's forecast for 1996/97. It said December's spending gap had been expected to swell following a shift in the timing of interest payments.

The ONS said much of the extra debt accrued in December was indeed due to large interest payments on government bonds, particularly strippable gilts. Interest payments totalled 3.09 billion pounds last month, compared with 1.93 billion in December last year.
Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets, said the gilt payments masked encouraging signs of moderating spending by government departments.
"Although total spending was pushed up by heavy interest payments on strippable gilts, departmental spending grew by just 0.7 percent year-on-year, the lowest growth for some months."
He said the government was well on track to hit its annual target and December's data did not signal an end to the recent improvement in Britain's public finances.

One feature of Friday's debt data was the disappointing crop of VAT, or value-added-tax, receipts harvested in December. Only 3.3 billion pounds of VAT was collected, down from 3.64 billion in December last year.
That, Coleman said, added to evidence from the Confederation of British Industry and the British Retail Consortium that retail sales in the run-up to Christmas were lacklustre.
"The disappointing return on VAT receipts may suggest a more subdued outturn for retail sales last month," he said.
CBI and BRC surveys for December both suggested retailers missed out on the pre-Christmas boom they had been counting on.
And consumer goods to homewear group Argos Plc and high street giant Sears Plc were forced to issue profit warnings after sales failed to meet expectations.

That evidence would have added weight to Chancellor Clarke's argument that interest rates should be left on hold. That was the decision following his monthly meeting with Bank of England governor Eddie George on Wednesday.
As for the government's finances, the pressure to raise departmental spending in the run-up to elections, due by May, has apparently failed to take hold.

But the jury will be out for a while yet. Andrew Milligan, economist at General Accident, said January and March were the key months for the PSBR as they benefit from a flood of corporation tax receipts.
"On current trends, the government is still on course for its target but January and March are the most important months."
